commenti.body:
Wonderful post. I saw this movie recently for the first time and loved it. I love how Johnny is so obviously intelligent, yet also spouting bullshit. And how the guard, less intelligent but wiser, instinctively sees through his bullshit 

I think the upshot of Johnny's character is that he needs mothering but all he can find is sex. I think it is implied that he was sexually abused by a woman. Notice how his mania has faded after sleeping nestled between Louise and Sophie. That's really what he needed, the whole movie

Excellent summation of the film but you fail to mention how absolutely hilarious it is. Did you not also find it funny? I was about Thewlis' age when the movie came out and the misanthropic nihilism was equally depressing and amusing. He's overly educated with no opportunity and a dismal view of the world. Highly verbose but emotionally stunted, and there are people in the film that are worse than he is.

Intelligent-but-powerless was my read. And the way this plays with various very different women.

I don't really have any good or articulate takes. I was so throttled by Johnny's complete and unconditional acceptance of pure cynicism I could not stop watching to find out what happens to him. And of course nothing does. The abuse he gives seems to imply he finds that behavior OK and must have been through it himself in some manner.

A reduction of life to such a crucible that pointlessness is the only possible perspective, thrust upon various unwitting people in various modes and contexts in their own lives.

I have been meaning to watch it again but i haven't seen it since around when it came out.

I see Johnny as a Holden Caulfield-like figure except that the source of his trauma is much less clear and as an adult, he is much more hurtful to the people around him. Whereas Holden accepts help at the end and seems to be healing, Johnny ultimately refuses help. I think it’s a combination of philosophical disagreement and self-punishment. He doesn’t think he (or anyone else maybe) deserves a good life, and so he can’t accept one. The last time I watched it, the security guards “Don’t waste your life” seemed quite poignant. The security guard may seem like he’s wasting his, but his dream of something better and his belief in being good to others keep him going and give his life purpose (like the James Thurber fable “The Moth and the Star”).

I didn’t think Johnny was especially intelligent or impressive. He’s just spewing out pseudo-intellectual nihilism, perhaps to make life as unbearable to others as it is to him, I don’t know. But as you pointed out, he doesn’t ever really say anything of substance. It’s the sort of simplistic quasi-philosophy you expect from someone who went to uni for a semester but never really understood the matter, only mastered the form. He keeps rambling about this and that, but nothing of substance *ever* comes out. I don’t believe he’d be a good psychologist at all. 

Granted, I have only watched it once and that was a year ago. I might misremember. Interesting post though

The movie can not be reduced to one simple idea, but one point that I've heard the director talk about, is the fact that Johnny is a man of very high intelligence, who because of his class situation, his position in life, his lack of formal education perhaps, has not found a way to turn this intelligence into something productive, something useful or creative. I think if you look at it like that from that angle, Johnny's neurosis becomes a bit more interpretable.

I saw the movie over a decade ago, but your posts rings true. I think there’s a substantial link between projected (or self-perceived) intelligence and the main character’s strain of depression/nihilism. This is hard to articulate, but there’s this *certainty* underlying the know-it-all posture of the holier than thou pessimist, and it can be part of a vicious cycle wherein you close yourself off to new ideas and perspectives… tragically insulating yourself from the ways of thinking that could let you actually enjoy life. That’s what I saw on display in Naked: a character study of a deeply hurt and frightened person who adopts superiority as a defense mechanism, walling themselves into a tower of doom and despair. They’re sure everything is shit, but at least they’re not playing the fool.

I found this movie late one night on IFC while tripping on LSD. 1/10 would not recommend.

David Thewlis is amazing. The movie is grimmy and dark with no joy to be found whatsoever. It is a well made miserable movie. If this kind of thing is your bag, then you will enjoy this movie.
that sounds like a truly awful experience
IDK, Johnny's pseudo intellectual monologues were hitting just right while under a head full. It was all of the rape and other nasty bits that were a bit draining.
Well put. I thoroughly enjoyed watching the film, as I have always had a fascination with stories from *the dark side* if you will. But not one part of me is impressed by the character of Johnny

Yep, it's a super interesting movie and it absolutely *nails* what is going for. It wasn't that pleasant for me to watch, and in retrospect I an appreciate that this is probably because the "aloof asshole" side of my personality felt a bit too called out, haha.
Yeah makes sense. I remember freaking out on mushrooms to a Linklater movie (Slacker)
I would have loved it

I think we get a hint of what was the source of his trauma in the scene where he has a mental breakdown and mentions his mother, IIRC. It was so raw and real and resonated with me a lot. 

Also, I got the impression that he runs away into the night at the end not because he feels like he doesn't deserve a good life – although there's indeed a lot of self-hate – but because his self-destructive tendencies are stronger than Louise's plans for a bright future; so to not drag her down along with himself, Johnny leaves her, out of love. 

The ending seemed ambiguous to me. Johnny's last interaction with the security guard who criticized his nihilism had a strong effect on him, as well as that fight with the waiter girl, so I think there's an implication that he might change for the better.

IMO, in this case the main character's nihilism works. Most of the times in cinema it doesn't as it needs to be justified, like it is justified with Rust Cohle in True Detective who is as nihilistic as it gets because he lost his wife and children and is investigating a child-trafficking satanistic ring. We don't have Johnny's background but it's clear that something happened and it won't let him go.

That's a pretty interesting comparison.

Rust has a seeming purpose that he has sort of identified though, whereas Johnny does not really seem to know what he is doing or the point of anything is.

> this was the most dream-like the movie got for me. There was a lot unstated. I think she was some sort of... expression of love

The fact she invited him over so willingly made it obvious to Johnny that she was sexually interested in him. However, after some initial prodding, Johnny quickly infers that she, in turn, is rather lonely and probably in need of human/emotional contact (just as he does, to a degree.) Their so-called uncomfortable silence together I took to be a quiet acknowledgment of this dynamic as if to say: "If I so choose, I know you will give yourself to me, but the only reason I haven't done so yet is because I don't feel like it (or because it would be too easy.") But then, once Johnny's questioning finally triggers her to cry, she retaliates, half-tired of being toyed with and half-frustrated at herself for allowing it. I suppose Johnny's little bow before leaving was a sign of remorsefulness but followed up with harsher words to recoil in defense.

I had this exact comparison in mind. Johnny seems to suffer from avoidant attachment wherein he longs for and is simultaneously afraid of human connection. He enjoys the hunt but pathologically leaves the carcass behind uneaten, consequently starving himself. This, in my mind, is a product of deep-seated trauma, as is in keeping with Caulfield.

Additionally, I do think Johnny is meant to be a kind of anti-Christ figure except instead of being evil he's just a complete failure of a savior. I bet he knows the damage he inflicts upon himself is compulsive and, going by his characters, kinda just shrugs it off as he does with everything else. He is hateful of himself and takes every opportunity he can to self-sabotage.

The failed-Christ angle is interesting. I hadn’t thought of that before. But the film did feel very inspired by Biblical themes, especially the white-clad roommate, who does charity work and seems to be a higher social class, returning to the flat and responding like a returning Christ or God seeing the mess humanity has made of things, failing to care for the world and letting the devil in.
